items.question: On 30 September 2026, the pass book shows a credit balance of ₹45,000. Cheques deposited but not yet collected: ₹12,000. Cheques issued but not yet presented: ₹8,000. A customer's direct deposit of ₹5,000 and bank charges of ₹500 are not yet in the cash book. What is the cash book balance before adjustments?
items.explanation: Cash book balance after correction equals ₹49,000 (pass book + uncollected cheques − unpresented cheques). Working back, remove the direct deposit and add back the bank charges, which the cash book has not yet recorded.

working.label: Less direct deposit, add bank charges

why_not.A: Deducted bank charges instead of adding them back while reversing to the old balance.
why_not.D: Stopped at the adjusted cash book balance and did not reverse the unrecorded items.
why_not.C: Added the direct deposit and deducted charges, reversing both adjustments the wrong way.

items.exam_tip: Items already in the cash book but not the pass book are timing items. Items missing from the cash book change its balance.
check_notes: Checker: Wording 'before adjustments' is slightly unclear; it means the cash book balance before recording the direct deposit and the bank charges.
Checker: Distractor D (49,000) is the adjusted cash book balance, so it is a plausible but wrong option. This is acceptable.
Checker: Students may confuse a credit balance in the pass book with an overdraft. The question is still unambiguous under standard convention.

items.question: On 31 March 2026, the cash book of Meera Traders shows a bank debit balance of ₹50,000. Cheques issued but not yet presented: ₹12,000. Cheques deposited but not yet credited by bank: ₹8,000. Bank charges ₹500 and interest credited ₹1,500 are not yet in cash book. Balance as per pass book is:
items.explanation: First correct the cash book for bank charges and interest. Then add back cheques issued but not presented, and deduct cheques deposited but not yet credited, to reach the pass book balance.

working.label: Less: deposited, not credited; Pass book

why_not.C: Ignored bank charges and interest, which are not yet in the cash book.
why_not.B: Reversed the treatment of both timing items: deducted issued cheques and added deposited ones.
why_not.D: Reversed the signs of bank charges and interest while adjusting the cash book.

items.exam_tip: Starting from cash book: items already in it but not in the bank are reversed; items only in the bank are adjusted first.
check_notes: Checker: The phrase 'credit' for the pass book balance may confuse some students, but it is standard and correct.
Checker: The wording 'bank debit balance' in the cash book is slightly informal but clear.

items.question: At 31 March 2026, a trader has three items. Item P: cost ₹80,000, NRV ₹72,000. Item Q: cost ₹1,20,000, NRV ₹1,35,000. Item R: cost ₹50,000, selling price ₹58,000, selling expenses ₹10,000. As per AS 2, closing inventory is:
items.explanation: AS 2 values inventory at lower of cost and NRV, item by item. NRV is selling price less estimated costs necessary to make the sale. Q stays at cost because its NRV is higher; unrealised gains are not recognised.

why_not.A: Takes all items at cost and ignores the write-down to NRV.
why_not.C: Takes R's NRV as selling price (₹58,000), forgetting to deduct selling expenses.
why_not.D: Takes higher of cost and NRV, which recognises unrealised gains.

items.exam_tip: NRV = selling price minus costs to sell. Then pick the lower of cost and NRV, item by item.

items.question: A firm uses 90,000 units of a material in FY 2025-26. Purchase price is ₹50 per unit, ordering cost is ₹250 per order and carrying cost is 10% of purchase price per unit per year. What is the total of ordering and carrying cost at EOQ?
items.explanation: Carrying cost per unit is ₹5. EOQ = √(2×90,000×250/5) = 3,000 units. Orders = 30, so ordering cost ₹7,500. Average stock 1,500 gives carrying cost ₹7,500. Total ₹15,000.

why_not.D: Counts only one component, ordering or carrying cost, not both.
why_not.B: Doubles the total, e.g. carrying cost on full EOQ instead of average stock.
why_not.C: Adds 1.5 times one component; mixes full and average stock wrongly.

items.exam_tip: At EOQ, ordering cost equals carrying cost. Find one and double it.

items.question: On 1 April 2026, Rao Ltd leases a machine for 2 years, paying ₹1,21,000 at the end of each year. Rate implicit in lease is 10%. Rao paid ₹10,000 initial direct costs and received ₹15,000 incentive from lessor on 1 April 2026. ROU asset at commencement is:
items.explanation: ROU asset = initial lease liability + initial direct costs + payments made at or before commencement − lease incentives received. Liability is the PV of payments at 10%: ₹2,10,000. So ROU = 2,10,000 + 10,000 − 15,000.

why_not.D: Takes the lease liability as ROU and ignores direct costs and incentive.
why_not.B: Adds direct costs but forgets to deduct the incentive received.
why_not.A: Adds the incentive instead of deducting it from the ROU asset.

items.exam_tip: ROU = liability + IDC + advance payments − incentives received. Costs go up, incentives come down.

items.topic: Foreign Exchange Risk - Interest Rate Parity
items.question: The spot rate is ₹84.00/USD. One-year risk-free rates are 10% p.a. in India and 5% p.a. in the USA. As per interest rate parity, what is the one-year forward rate (₹/USD)?
items.explanation: Under interest rate parity, forward = spot × (1 + rate of quoted currency) / (1 + rate of base currency). Here INR is the quoted currency, so the Indian rate goes in the numerator. The USD trades at a premium because India's interest rate is higher.

why_not.A: Inverted the ratio, putting the US rate in the numerator; this gives a discount for USD.
why_not.B: Added the US rate to spot (84 × 1.05) and ignored the Indian rate.
why_not.C: Used only the Indian rate (84 × 1.10) and ignored the US rate.

items.exam_tip: Higher-interest currency trades at a forward discount; here INR is weaker, so the forward ₹/USD is above spot.
